# FlutterGuard - full reference

> See what ships in your Flutter app. FlutterGuard inspects Flutter Android APKs through an Android app or a source-built CLI. Both use one JVM detection engine and report manifest policy, compiled Dart strings, assets, dependencies, endpoints and signing evidence. MIT licensed.
>
> Canonical: https://flutterguard.dev/
> CLI guide: https://flutterguard.dev/cli/
> Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.flutterguard.app
> Latest GitHub release: https://github.com/anasfik/FlutterGuard/releases/latest
> Source (MIT): https://github.com/anasfik/FlutterGuard
> Engine source: https://github.com/anasfik/FlutterGuard/tree/main/engine
> Privacy: https://flutterguard.dev/privacy/
> About: https://flutterguard.dev/about/
> Contact: https://flutterguard.dev/contact/

## What it is

FlutterGuard is for people who ship Flutter apps and want to see what a release exposes before someone else does. You point it at an installed Flutter app or a single APK. The Android app runs on the phone; the CLI runs the same engine on a plain JVM. Both turn static evidence into findings and a triage grade.

The Android flow has three steps:

1. Discover: list the Flutter apps installed on this device, or pick a single APK.
2. Inspect: read the SDK versions, endpoints and exposed strings inside the release.
3. Report: save the evidence and return to it later.

Flutter-aware inspection matters because a Flutter release carries clues in its compiled library and asset bundle, not just its permissions. FlutterGuard reads these layers alongside SDK versions, embedded endpoints, exposed strings, AI providers, signing information and network policy.

Maintainer: Anas Fikhi, Flutter and Software Engineer.

## Install and distribution

- Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer.
- Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.flutterguard.app
- GitHub releases: https://github.com/anasfik/FlutterGuard/releases/latest
- No account and no paid tier.

Channel status as last observed:

- GitHub releases contain the Android APK and a source-built CLI.
- Google Play is updated separately; its current version is not verified here. Do not assume feature parity between channels.
- Play and GitHub use separate signing channels. Some older GitHub builds used an older key. Moving from one of those builds requires uninstalling the app, which deletes local reports, history and settings. Exporting a report does not restore that history.
- Uninstalling deletes local reports, history and settings. Exporting a report is not a history restore.

The CLI is not distributed as a binary. See the CLI section.

## The CLI

The CLI is a thin terminal entry point over the shared engine. It reads a package without executing it and needs no phone, emulator or Android device.

Build from source:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/anasfik/FlutterGuard.git
cd FlutterGuard
echo "sdk.dir=$ANDROID_HOME" > local.properties
./gradlew :cli:installDist
cli/build/install/flutterguard/bin/flutterguard --help
```

- JDK 17 or newer is required.
- The repository build also configures the Android app module, so use the Android SDK setup described in the project README.
- The launcher contains the engine, `org.json` and `kotlinx-coroutines-core`. The scanning machine does not need the Android SDK.
- `--help` prints the usage line and exits 2.

Scan contract:

```
flutterguard scan INPUT.apk --json OUTPUT.json [--sarif OUTPUT.sarif] [--fail-on confirmed]
```

Output rules:

- Create the output parent directory first; it must already exist.
- The destination files must not already exist. The CLI refuses to overwrite and exits 2.
- Use fresh filenames for each run, for example with a UTC timestamp, or write to a fresh directory.
- New output is staged as sibling temporary files, flushed, then published with atomic moves. A destination that appears during the scan is refused, and a failed publication rolls back what was already written.

Exit codes:

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| 0 | Scan completed; the gate was not requested or was not hit. |
| 1 | Scan completed and `--fail-on confirmed` found at least one confirmed finding. |
| 2 | Invalid arguments, unreadable or unsupported input, scan failure, cancellation or output failure. |

The gate is evaluated after both outputs are published, so exit 1 cannot hide a scan or write error.

Outputs:

- `--json` writes the engine's redacted report, schema `flutterguard/report/2`. Detected secret values are masked and never written to disk by the CLI.
- `--sarif` writes one run of SARIF 2.1.0 in the GitHub code-scanning shape. There is one rule per distinct finding id, with a title, remediation text and severity level. Results carry a rule id, level, scrubbed message, partial fingerprint and one location.
- SARIF locations point at the APK as a `file:` URI with no region or line data. The artifact is a binary; invented source positions would be false precision.
- Fingerprints use `findingId|evidence.source` and contain no secret value, snippet or hash of one.
- Confirmed critical and high findings are errors; confirmed medium and low are warnings; confirmed informational and every suspected finding are notes. Inventory is omitted by default.
- Progress and errors go to stderr. stdout stays empty, and progress lines carry only a stage name and percentage.

CI:

- `.github/workflows/apk-scan.yml` sets up JDK 17, runs the CLI tests, builds the distribution, builds FlutterGuard's own debug APK as an owned fixture, scans it to JSON and SARIF, and retains both as workflow artifacts for 14 days.
- A separate job uploads the SARIF to code scanning and is the only one granted `security-events: write`. Fork pull requests skip it.
- The workflow does not use `--fail-on` on its own fixture because a debug build legitimately contains confirmed findings such as a debuggable manifest and a debug certificate.
- Local SARIF validation is not GitHub acceptance. Security-tab ingestion, alert display and fingerprint deduplication are unverified until the workflow runs on GitHub with those permissions.

CLI limits:

- One APK per invocation; split APK sets are not assembled.
- No comparison command. Release comparisons happen in the Android app.
- No decompilation. Snapshot metadata describes the library build; it is not Dart source and does not definitively prove obfuscation.
- No standalone engine SDK and no Maven or JitPack package.
- Static evidence does not prove exploitability.

## The engine

The engine is a repository module at https://github.com/anasfik/FlutterGuard/tree/main/engine. It is a plain JVM library used by both the Android app and the CLI. It is not a separately published SDK.

## What it reads

1. APK container: entries, sizes, compression, bundled assets, native libraries and ABIs.
2. AndroidManifest: package and version data, SDK levels, permissions, exported activities, services, receivers and providers, cleartext and backup settings, deep links and debug flags.
3. Release contents: hosts, endpoints, URLs, keys and configuration values that shipped inside the APK, plus the SDKs they belong to.
4. libapp.so: strings and symbols inside the AOT machine code.
5. Signing data: certificate identity and structural properties of the signature scheme.
6. Route-like strings: candidate screen and route names found as strings in the binary.
7. Snapshot metadata: how the Dart library was built. It is not decompilation and is not a definitive obfuscation verdict.

## Confidence and grades

- Confirmed findings are artifact facts read directly from the package.
- Suspected matches are leads worth checking.
- Inventory lists what is present without judging it.
- Only confirmed findings affect the grade.
- A-F are triage labels, not a security certificate. A confirmed finding does not prove exploitability, credential validity or endpoint reachability, and an A is not a guarantee of safety.

## Android release comparisons

The Android app compares two saved scans of the same package. It shows what arrived and what left across permissions, endpoints, SDK and dependency markers, native libraries, signing certificates, network policy and findings. If a category could not be read in one scan, the comparison says so instead of claiming nothing changed. A scan of a different package is refused. There is no CLI comparison command.

## Offline and network behaviour

- Android scans run locally because the app declares no INTERNET permission.
- CLI scans read the artifact locally and write reports where you point them.
- Building either project may download dependencies; CI jobs may upload artifacts according to their own workflow policy.
- Scanning is local; build and CI are separate network boundaries.

## Android privacy

- No account, no sign-in, no advertising SDK and no crash reporter.
- The app or APK you open stays on the device.
- Reports and history live in private app storage.
- A report leaves the device only when you explicitly export it and choose a destination.
- Uninstalling FlutterGuard deletes those private reports and history.

## Limits

- Static analysis is evidence, not proof. A finding shows what is present in the release, not that it is exploitable.
- No runtime hooking, no traffic interception, no authentication testing. The tools do not run the target or observe its traffic.
- libapp.so is AOT machine code. String literals and symbols are readable; Dart source is not recovered.
- Routes are candidate strings, not a navigation graph.
- AABs are not supported. Convert an AAB to APKs with bundletool first.
- The signature check is structural: it inspects what the APK contains and does not prove the signer's identity.
- Some ROMs block APK reads, which can prevent or limit a scan.
- Scan only apps you own or have permission to test.
- The CLI does not compare releases, assemble split APKs or ship as a package.

## FAQ

### Is FlutterGuard free?

Yes. It is open source under the MIT licence, with no account, no ads and no paid tier.

### Does the Android app need an internet connection?

No. The app has no INTERNET permission, so scans run entirely on the device.

### Does the CLI need an internet connection?

The scan is local. Building may download Gradle dependencies, and a CI job may upload artifacts under its own policy.

### Which apps can it check?

Flutter apps you own or are authorised to test, either installed on the device or supplied as a single APK.

### Does a finding prove the app is exploitable?

No. Findings are static evidence from the release, not a confirmed exploit.

### Where do updates come from?

Google Play and GitHub releases. The channels have different versions and signing keys; check the version you installed.

## Guides and pages

- [Flutter security: what a release APK exposes](https://flutterguard.dev/flutter-security/): manifest, endpoint, string, dependency and signing checks that matter in a shipped Flutter app.
- [Flutter APK inspection: reading a release on Android](https://flutterguard.dev/flutter-apk-inspection/): a phone workflow, terminal commands and triage rules that avoid false alarms.
- [ProGuard for Flutter: what R8 and obfuscation hide](https://flutterguard.dev/proguard-flutter/): Android shrinking versus Dart obfuscation, and what remains readable in libapp.so.
- [MobSF alternative for auditing Flutter APKs](https://flutterguard.dev/mobsf-alternative/): where a broader mobile platform ends and a Flutter release begins, and when each tool fits.
- [Flutter app security audit checklist](https://flutterguard.dev/flutter-security-checklist/): a per-release checklist for artifact identity, manifest policy, exposed data, dependencies, endpoints, signing and handover.
- [What 26 released Flutter apps expose](https://flutterguard.dev/flutter-release-corpus/): measured results from public release APKs, with method and limits.
- [FlutterGuard CLI: scan Flutter APKs in CI](https://flutterguard.dev/cli/): source build, scan flags, output paths, exit codes, SARIF and CI limits.
- [Changelog](https://flutterguard.dev/changelog/): dated release notes, plus an [Atom feed](https://flutterguard.dev/feed.xml).

- [Contact](https://flutterguard.dev/contact/)

## Licence and legal

FlutterGuard is MIT licensed. Use it only on applications you own or are authorised to test. Findings are evidence for your own review and are not an authorisation to test third-party apps or infrastructure.
